title: Diagnostic Foundations
summary: A repeatable observation-first workflow for separating environmental, root-zone, nutritional, pest, pathogen, and physical causes before choosing a response.
whatToLookFor: Where symptoms began: old growth, new growth, upper canopy, lower canopy, roots, flowers, or one branch
Pattern: uniform, interveinal, marginal, spotted, distorted, wilted, asymmetric, or localized
Progression: sudden, gradual, spreading, stable, or recovering
Recent changes in irrigation, nutrition, environment, lighting, handling, or sanitation
lookAlikes: Different problems can create similar yellowing, spotting, curling, wilting, or stunting
A single photograph rarely establishes cause
confirmWith: Inspect roots, stems, leaf undersides, and affected flowers
Record substrate moisture, pH, EC, air temperature, RH, leaf temperature when available, and light context
Use magnification when pests or fungal structures are plausible
Compare affected and unaffected plants and locations
managementPrinciples: Correct the highest-confidence underlying cause rather than chasing a symptom
Change one major variable at a time when practical so the response is interpretable
Document the intervention and reassess progression

title: Two-Spotted Spider Mite
summary: A common mite pest that feeds by piercing plant cells. Early infestations may appear as fine stippling; webbing is usually a later, heavier-infestation sign rather than a requirement for diagnosis.
whatToLookFor: Fine pale stippling that can merge into bronzing as injury accumulates
Mites and spherical eggs concentrated on leaf undersides
Fine webbing when populations become high
Hot, dry locations may show faster population growth
confirmWith: Inspect leaf undersides with a hand lens or microscope
Look for moving mites plus eggs rather than relying on webbing alone
Sample several leaves from symptom edges and apparently healthy areas
managementPrinciples: Remove or isolate heavily infested material when appropriate
Use a compatible integrated program rather than repeating one control tactic
Target leaf undersides and repeat scouting because eggs and hidden individuals can survive incomplete coverage
prevention: Keep benches and plant debris clean
Avoid moving from infested areas into clean areas without sanitation

title: Thrips
summary: Small, slender insects whose feeding can leave silvery or pale scars, distorted tissue, and dark fecal specks. Species and life cycles vary, so identification should be based on the organism as well as damage.
whatToLookFor: Silvery, scraped, or pale feeding scars
Small dark fecal specks near feeding damage
Slender mobile insects in flowers, new growth, or leaf surfaces
Distortion when young tissue is attacked
confirmWith: Use magnification to locate insects
Tap foliage over a light-colored surface or inspect sticky cards as a monitoring aid
Check flowers and growing tips in addition to mature leaves
managementPrinciples: Base management on confirmed presence and life stage
Combine sanitation, exclusion, monitoring, and compatible biological or other controls
Continue monitoring after visible injury stops because damage can outlast the insects that caused it
prevention: Control weeds and alternate hosts near production areas
Use clean tools and workflow separation

title: Fungus Gnats
summary: Small flies associated with moist organic substrates. Adults are primarily a monitoring nuisance; larvae inhabit the root zone and can feed on fungi, organic matter, and tender roots, with the greatest concern in seedlings and stressed plants.
whatToLookFor: Small dark adults running or flying near the substrate surface
Larvae that are translucent to whitish with a dark head capsule
Persistent surface moisture or organic buildup
Weak seedlings or root injury when larval pressure is high
lookAlikes: Root decline caused by overwatering or pathogens without gnats
confirmWith: Use sticky cards to monitor adults
Inspect the upper root zone or use a simple larval monitoring method
Distinguish larvae morphologically rather than assuming every small fly is a fungus gnat
managementPrinciples: Correct chronic excess moisture where compatible with crop needs
Reduce algae and decomposing organic material
Use an integrated larval-management program when populations justify action

title: Aphids
summary: Sap-feeding insects that often cluster on tender growth and leaf undersides. Honeydew, cast skins, and colonies are stronger evidence than leaf curl alone.
whatToLookFor: Clusters of soft-bodied insects on stems, petioles, undersides, and growing tips
Sticky honeydew and sometimes secondary sooty growth
White cast skins near colonies
Distorted or slowed young growth under heavier feeding
lookAlikes: Non-pest debris or shed plant tissue
confirmWith: Use magnification to inspect body shape and cornicles when visible
Check both winged and wingless forms
Inspect roots if root aphids are a possibility
managementPrinciples: Treat colonies early and monitor new growth
Use compatible biological, physical, and other controls as part of an integrated program
Address ant activity where it protects aphids
prevention: Maintain clean work flow between rooms

title: Broad and Russet Mites
summary: Extremely small mites that can produce severe distortion, bronzing, shortened internodes, and abnormal new growth. Symptoms are not specific enough for a visual-only diagnosis.
whatToLookFor: Distorted, hardened, twisted, or unusually small new growth
Bronzing or russeting of affected tissues
Abnormal flower or shoot development
Damage concentrated in rapidly growing tissues
confirmWith: Use sufficient magnification to locate the mites or their eggs
Collect multiple samples from symptomatic growing points
Do not diagnose from leaf shape alone
managementPrinciples: Isolate suspect plants while confirming
Use an integrated plan suited to the identified mite and production system
Re-scout new growth because damaged tissue will not return to normal shape
prevention: Control movement of tools and personnel between plant groups

title: Powdery Mildew
summary: A group of obligate fungal pathogens that produce superficial white growth on susceptible tissues. Early colonies can be small and easy to confuse with residues, so confirmation matters.
whatToLookFor: White powdery colonies that expand across leaves or other susceptible tissues
Colonies that may begin as isolated circular or irregular patches
Repeated appearance on new tissues after incomplete control
confirmWith: Inspect with magnification for fungal structures
Compare suspected colonies before and after gentle wiping
Check multiple canopy zones and nearby plants
managementPrinciples: Remove heavily affected tissue where appropriate without spreading spores
Improve environmental and canopy conditions that favor repeated disease pressure
Use a rotation of compatible management tools rather than relying on one repeated input
prevention: Avoid carrying contaminated material into clean rooms

title: Botrytis / Gray Mold
summary: Botrytis cinerea can colonize senescent or injured tissues and cause destructive flower rot under favorable conditions. Internal flower damage can be advanced before surface sporulation is obvious.
whatToLookFor: Localized browning, softening, or collapse within flowers
Gray-brown sporulation under suitable conditions
Dead leaf tips or damaged tissue embedded in dense flowers
Rapid progression in humid, poorly ventilated microclimates
confirmWith: Inspect inside affected flower clusters rather than only the surface
Use magnification for characteristic fungal structures when possible
Record humidity, condensation, airflow, and recent wetting events
managementPrinciples: Remove affected material carefully to reduce dispersal
Correct moisture and airflow problems
Do not retain visibly moldy harvested material for consumption
prevention: Sanitize dead tissue and plant debris

title: Damping-Off Complex
summary: A seedling disease syndrome caused by several soilborne fungi and oomycetes. It can occur before emergence or after emergence when the stem or root tissues are attacked.
whatToLookFor: Seedlings that fail to emerge despite viable seed
Water-soaked or constricted tissue near the media line
Seedlings that topple after stem weakening
Root discoloration or decay in propagation media
lookAlikes: Seedling collapse from extreme salinity or other abiotic stress
confirmWith: Inspect stem base and roots closely
Review moisture, temperature, sanitation, and media history
Laboratory diagnosis may be needed to identify the causal organism
managementPrinciples: Remove collapsed seedlings and contaminated debris
Avoid chronic saturation
Improve propagation sanitation and air exchange
Use organism-specific management when the pathogen is confirmed
prevention: Use clean propagation equipment and media
Provide suitable temperature and oxygen conditions
Sanitize trays and tools between batches

title: Root Disease Complex
summary: Root decline can involve oomycetes, fungi, low oxygen, temperature stress, salinity, chronic saturation, or combinations of these factors. Brown roots alone do not identify a pathogen.
whatToLookFor: Loss of fine roots or root-tip integrity
Soft, sloughing, discolored, or poorly branched roots
Reduced water uptake, wilting, or slowed growth despite moist media
Root-zone odor or biofilm changes that require context rather than instant diagnosis
lookAlikes: Normal staining from some substrates or inputs
Low oxygen without an infectious pathogen
confirmWith: Examine root texture and fine-root structure, not color alone
Measure root-zone moisture, EC, pH, and temperature
Review irrigation frequency and oxygen conditions
Use laboratory testing when organism identification matters
managementPrinciples: Restore appropriate root-zone aeration and irrigation first when those are clearly abnormal
Remove severely compromised plants when they threaten the rest of the crop
Use pathogen-specific measures only when supported by evidence
prevention: Maintain clean irrigation and propagation systems
Prevent cross-contamination through shared runoff or tools

title: Hop Latent Viroid (HLVd)
summary: Hop latent viroid is an infectious RNA agent documented in cannabis. Symptoms can include reduced vigor and yield, but plants may also be asymptomatic; visual inspection cannot confirm infection.
whatToLookFor: Unexplained loss of vigor or reduced performance in some infected plants
Inconsistent expression, including plants with few obvious visual symptoms
Patterns associated with shared propagation material or contaminated cutting practices
confirmWith: Use validated laboratory testing such as appropriate nucleic-acid amplification assays
Test source plants and propagation stock rather than relying on symptoms
Investigate sanitation and propagation links among positives
managementPrinciples: Isolate confirmed positives
Use clean tested stock for propagation
Follow validated sanitation procedures for cutting tools and propagation workflows
prevention: Establish testing protocols for mother stock
Sanitize tools between plants using validated methods

title: Abiotic vs Biotic Damage
summary: Environmental and root-zone disorders can mimic pest and disease symptoms. Distribution, timing, progression, and direct evidence help distinguish them.
whatToLookFor: Uniform damage across plants exposed to the same environment or irrigation event
Sharp boundaries that match light, spray, airflow, or wetting patterns
Presence or absence of organisms, sporulation, frass, eggs, webbing, or lesions
Whether symptoms continue spreading after the suspected abiotic event has ended
lookAlikes: Nutrient availability disorders versus root disease
Light or heat injury versus mite damage
confirmWith: Map symptoms spatially
Inspect with magnification
Compare environmental and irrigation records
Use laboratory testing when a systemic or microbial cause remains plausible
managementPrinciples: Do not apply pest or disease controls without evidence
Correct measurable environmental or root-zone problems when present
Reassess whether new symptoms are still appearing
prevention: Document sprays, sanitation, irrigation, and handling events

title: Scouting and Sampling
summary: Good diagnostics depend on representative observations. A repeatable scouting route, consistent sample locations, magnification, and records are more useful than occasional symptom photos.
whatToLookFor: Changes from the previous inspection
Hot spots near doors, vents, propagation areas, irrigation issues, or dense canopy zones
Upper and lower leaf surfaces
Roots, stems, flowers, media surface, traps, and surrounding weeds or ornamentals
lookAlikes: Sampling only damaged leaves can exaggerate severity
Sampling only healthy canopy tops can miss early infestations below
confirmWith: Use the same route and observation points on a schedule
Record counts or severity consistently
Photograph the same locations over time
Retain samples when laboratory testing may be needed
managementPrinciples: Use trends, not isolated observations
Increase inspection frequency around confirmed hot spots
Separate monitoring data from treatment decisions so efficacy can be judged
prevention: Train scouts on pest life stages and symptom vocabulary
Keep hand lenses and traps available
Maintain clean records linked to plant groups or rooms

title: Sanitation and Quarantine
summary: Exclusion and workflow design are often more reliable than trying to eradicate a problem after it spreads. Quarantine, clean-to-dirty movement, and validated tool sanitation reduce transmission opportunities.
whatToLookFor: Shared tools moving between plant groups
Uncontrolled incoming clones or plants
Plant debris, standing water, algae, and hard-to-clean surfaces
People or equipment moving from affected areas into clean areas
lookAlikes: A visually clean surface is not necessarily sanitized
A symptom-free incoming plant is not necessarily pest- or pathogen-free
confirmWith: Audit movement pathways
Verify sanitation products and contact procedures are appropriate for the target
Use testing or extended observation for high-risk incoming stock
managementPrinciples: Move from clean areas toward suspect or affected areas when possible
Dedicate tools or sanitize between plant groups
Remove waste without carrying it through clean production zones
prevention: Train everyone who handles plants on movement boundaries
